title: Coordinated tag/semver/hash pin semantics for model onboarding and runtime resolution
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: As we onboard a growing catalog of community and partner models we need a single, predictable semantics surface for pinning model versions in the Redwood API and SDKs. Current behavior differs between SDKs and the runtime: some clients allow tag aliases (eg 'stable'), some allow naive semver ranges, and others require immutable commit refs. This inconsistency causes surprise rollouts, failed regressions tests, and operator confusion when runtime fallbacks pick a different variant than the client expected.

Problem statement: Define and implement deterministic resolution rules that support three common pin forms (named tag, semver/range, immutable ref/hash) while preserving backwards compatibility with existing shorthand pins and allowing explicit server-side policy overrides. Additionally we must publish model performance profiles (latency/cost/throughput) for the resolved variant at onboarding time and surface these to SDKs and the Console for decisioning.

Goals:
- Single documented resolution algorithm used by all SDKs and the runtime.
- Allow clients to express intent: strict (must match exact ref), flexible (accept compatible semver ranges), or prefer-latest (resolve to tag alias).
- Runtime fallbacks (eg when a pinned ref is unavailable) must be explicit and auditable.
- Performance profiles for the resolved binary/quantization variant must be published and version-linked so customers can reason about cost and latency differences across pins.
- Minimal breaking changes for existing customers; graceful migration path.

Proposal (high level):
1) Pin forms accepted in request payloads and SDK constructors:
   - ref:<sha>  (immutable commit hash, highest precedence)
   - semver:<range>  (compatible semver ranges, eg semver:^1.2.0)
   - tag:<name>  (release-like aliases maintained by onboarding tooling, eg tag:stable or tag:fast)
   - legacy: <string>  (legacy shorthand like "gpt-4o" retains backward compat but is normalized server-side)

2) Resolution precedence (deterministic order):
   a) ref:<sha> resolves immediately to the matching artifact if available. Failure -> explicit fallback rules.
   b) semver:<range> resolves by matching highest semver-compatible released artifact (prefers stable builds over canary with the same semver tag).
   c) tag:<name> resolves using the tag manifest created by the onboarding pipeline (tag manifests are immutable snapshots pointing to a list of artifact refs with stability metadata).
   d) legacy shorthand is normalized to one of the above at the API ingress layer; normalization is logged.

3) Client-side vs server-side resolution:
   - SDKs MAY attempt to resolve semver ranges locally using a cached manifest to provide earlier validation and improved latency on preflight checks.
   - Final authoritative resolution happens in the control plane; SDKs must accept the resolved_ref returned in the response and reconcile local cache.

4) Fallback & policy model:
   - Request MAY include a policy block: {"fallback": "none|compatible-semv|tag:stable|latest"}.
   - Fallbacks are auditable and must appear in request/response logs and Console rollouts.
   - If fallback is 'none' and resolution fails, return 409 with a descriptive resolution_error and no runtime fallback.

5) Performance profile publishing:
   - Onboarding pipeline will run perf harnesses producing artifact-level profiles: median latency (p50/p95), cost-per-token estimate, throughput numbers for typical batch sizes, supported quantization settings, and recommended batch sizes.
   - Profiles are attached to the artifact ref and published to the model catalog and Console.
   - The SDK will expose a lightweight API to fetch the profile for a resolved_ref so client-side adaptive batching/cost-estimates can use authoritative numbers.

6) Telemetry & audit: every resolution must emit a standard resolution event: {request_pin, resolved_ref, resolution_path, perf_profile_id, resolution_latency_ms}. This will feed the Console trace and rollout analysis.

API examples (proposal JSON shape):
POST /v1/requests
{
  "model_pin": "semver:^2.1.0",
  "pin_policy": "prefer_strict",
  "fallback": "compatible-semv",
  "input": "..."
}
Response:
{
  "resolved_ref": "ref:abc123def456",
  "resolved_manifest": "manifest:2026-02-24-3",
  "perf_profile_id": "perf-ml-2026-02-24-3"
}

Acceptance constraints (see below) ensure SDKs and runtime implement this surface.

Migration notes: Normalization of legacy shorthand will be enabled behind a feature-flag for 2 release cycles. We'll ship server-side logging for three weeks before flipping normalization to allow teams to detect regressions. SDKs will include a deprecation warning if they send legacy pins without explicit normalization.

Storage/schema changes: add artifact-level perf_profile_id and tag manifest table (immutable snapshots). Backfill plan: run onboarding perf jobs for top 50 customer-used models first (safety-first).

Open questions / Trade-offs:
- Local SDK resolution vs always-server: local resolution improves early UX but risks cache drift; mitigation: use ETags and explicit reconcile responses.
- Semver semantics for pre-releases: currently we propose to treat pre-releases as lower precedence unless "prefer_canary" policy set.
- Rollout complexity for tag reassignment: tagging operations must produce a new immutable manifest; tag mutation is allowed but results in new manifest id to keep auditability.

Next steps:
- Implement server-side manifest and perf profile schema (ENG-119001)
- Add SDK normalization & reconcile hooks (ENG-119002)
acceptance_criteria: Authoritative resolution implemented in control plane and returns resolved_ref in every request response (no silent fallbacks)
SDKs expose getResolvedProfile(resolved_ref) and reconcile cache on response (JS, Python first)
Onboarding pipeline attaches perf_profile_id to artifact and Console displays perf profile for resolved variants
Fallback policy honored and logged; 'none' returns 409 with descriptive payload
Backwards compatibility: legacy shorthand normalization can be toggled and emits deprecation warnings
